Findings and conclusions: The mean elimination half-life for methamphetamine is approximately 10 hours, with considerable inter-individual variability in pharmacokinetics. A narrative review taking into account forensic issues Abstract Driving under the influence of alcohol has been shown to increase the risk of involvement in road traffic collisions (RTCs) however, less is known about the effects of illicit drugs, and a clear correlation between drug concentrations and RTC risk is still debated. The goal of this narrative review is to assess the current literature regarding the most detected psychoactive drugs in RTC (ethanol, amphetamines, cannabis, opioids and cocaine), in relation to driving performance. Evidence on impaired driving due to psychoactive substances, forensic issues relating to the assessment of the impact of drugs, blood cut-off values proposed to date as well as scientific basis for proposed legislative limits are discussed. At present there is no unequivocal evidence demonstrating a clear dose/concentration dependent impairment in many substances. Per se and zero tolerance approaches seem to have negative effect on drugged driving fatalities. However, the weight of these approaches needs further investigation. Keywords: Alcohol, Cannabis, Opioids, Cocaine, Driving under the influence of drugs, Drug legislation Highlights * • Driving under the influence of psychotropic substances has become a widespread phenomenon. * • Only a few substances have been reported to have a clear dose/concentration dependent impairment. * • Statistically significant differences should not be considered as clinically significant per se * • There is wide variability in legislative cut-offs. * • Detection limits seems to be the most public safety-oriented legislative approach. 1. Introduction According to the WHO, road traffic collisions (RTC) account for about 1.3 million deaths and 20–50 million non-fatal injuries worldwide [1] and all over the world driving under the influence of psychotropic substances has become a widespread phenomenon. Despite driving under the influence of alcohol (DUIA) has been shown to increase the risk of involvement in RTCs, with relative risk increasing with blood alcohol concentration [2], less is known about the effects of medicinal and illicit drugs [3], and a clear correlation between drug concentrations and RTC risk is still debated [3,4]. Actually, the association between such substances (especially alcohol, amphetamines, cannabis, opioids and cocaine), impaired driving and road accidents has been extensively investigated so far [3], with results stating a link to an increased risk of car crashes and serious injuries not only to the impaired driver but also to other people, constituting a threat for public safety [5]. Indeed, the assumption of these substances may impair the visual, cognitive, and/or motor abilities needed for safe driving [6]. A recent review published by Kwon and Han [7] showed that in Europe most of the studies on blood toxicological results are performed in northern countries, such as Norway [8,9], Germany [10], Sweden [11], Finland [12,13], Switzerland [14], Poland [15], UK [16], and Denmark [17], while fewer studies report blood results from southern European countries [6]. Over the years, countries have developed different strategies in order to face this relevant issue. For example, recently Norway and Sweden adopted a “zero tolerance approach” toward driving under the influence of psychoactive substances which has led to a reduction of positive cases [6], while other countries have introduced threshold limits. Alcohol is the only substance for which official international cut-off values have been clearly proposed, as well as standardized analytical methods. Indeed, for what concerns other substances, straightforward cut-off values are not available as a consequence of the heterogeneity of results in published studies and different involved approaches. In fact, even though blood is the gold standard matrix for drug confirmation and quantification analysis in DUID cases as the values found are considered to be closely related to current pharmacological effects on the central nervous system, a comparison between different proposed cut-off values evidenced great dissimilarity internationally [18]. Given the wide variability not only in the indicated cut-offs but also in the effects of the substances themselves, the authors present a summary of the results of studies on the subject, with emphasis on forensic aspects, to deepen the understanding of such a complex issue. The purpose of this narrative review is to evaluate current literature regarding the most detected psychoactive drugs in RTC, which are ethanol, amphetamines, cannabis, opioids and cocaine in relation to driving performance and traffic safety; benzodiazepines have not been included because of the wide differences between the various types. Limitations of current legal approaches in this area are considered. The scientific basis for the proposed legislative limits is presented and recent evidence on impaired driving due to psychoactive substances is reported, as well as blood cut-off values proposed to date. 2. Keywords were searched individually and in association with each of the others. Only full text articles manuscripts in English have been included. fetched_contents.text: Injury associated with methamphetamine use: A review of the literature Abstract This paper reviews the literature exploring issues around methamphetamine and injury. There was a paucity of peer reviewed quantitative research and a lack of large scale epidemiological studies. Further sources described cases and others described injury risk as part of an overall review of methamphetamine misuse. Thus, a number of limitations and potential biases exist within the literature. The main areas where associations were noted or extrapolated with methamphetamine use and injury were around driving and violence. Other associations with injury related to methamphetamine manufacture. There was also circumstantial evidence for third party injury (that is injury to those not specifically involved in drug use or drug manufacture); however, the available data are inadequate to confirm these associations/risks. Introduction Methamphetamine is a stimulant drug with high dependence liability, and is a commonly misused illicit substance worldwide. The drug first appeared as a legal drug in nasal decongestant preparations during the 1930s, but methamphetamine has been used for non-medical purposes wherever it has been readily available. Methamphetamine is a powerful psychostimulant which has a high dependence liability [1,2] and can be readily manufactured from precursor substances which are common ingredients of 'over the counter' cold remedies [3,4]. Methamphetamine can be smoked, snorted, injected or swallowed and its effects can last up to 12 hours. The desired effects from the use of illicit methamphetamine include euphoria, decreased need for food and sleep, increased mental alertness and energy levels, disinhibition, sense of wellbeing and increased confidence [5]. Effects are dose-dependent and onset ranges from 20–40 minutes if swallowed, 3–5 minutes when snorted, and almost immediately if smoked or taken intravenously. Smoking and injecting users report an intensely pleasurable wave of sensation or 'rush' [6]. Repeated and chronic use of methamphetamine may result in undesirable and dangerous effects including psychotic symptoms such as severe paranoia, hallucinations and delusions of persecution, anxiety symptoms, agitation and affective symptoms such as depression and mood swings [3,7,8]. Other reported effects of chronic use include insomnia, malnutrition, involuntary movements, increased psychomotor activity, elevated blood pressure and heart rate sometimes resulting in myocardial infarction or stroke [9-12]. Continued use has a high dependence probability [4]. The most common symptoms of withdrawal from use are depression, [2,13] fatigue, restlessness, nervousness, feelings of alienation and irritation, craving for more methamphetamine, severe paranoia, hallucinations and delusions [14-16]. The physical effects of withdrawal can include tremor, sweating, headaches, dizziness, dry mouth and gastrointestinal problems. Severity of withdrawal depends on length and magnitude of use [5] and may be compounded by any pre-existing mental health problems [17]. The purpose of this paper is to provide a critical review of the English language peer reviewed and 'grey' literature on the association between methamphetamine use and injury. Literature reviewed for this paper The Medline, Embase, PsychInfo, ERIC and Factiva databases were searched over the period 1997 to 2005 for references to injuries and other harms related to methamphetamine or "P' use. Key terms included: methamphetamine, street drugs (ice, crank, pure or crystal meth), or illicit drugs combined with injur$, harm$ or risk$. Search terms varied slightly depending on terminology used in individual databases. In addition the websites of drug agencies such as the United National Office for Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), and the Australian Crime Commission were searched for relevant reports. Key studies were checked for further references. Additional material was sourced from those working in the drug misuse and control fields in New Zealand. The result was the creation of an Endnote database containing 174 references to research, information bulletins and reports and other relevant publications on the topic of methamphetamine or 'P' use and its potential for harm to the user and others, including children and emergency service workers. Much of the available evidence on which this review has been based is of limited scope and variable quality in terms of gold standard research. In practice we found no population-based studies or large trials which provided insight into the burden of methamphetamine use and its association with injury. Evidence linking methamphetamine use to crash or incident rates is mixed but suggestive of increased risk overall. A 1996 study of 28 cases of drivers arrested or killed in traffic accidents who tested positive for methamphetamine concluded that methamphetamine was implicated in those outcomes [N3-R1]. Another review of injury literature reports that methamphetamine is associated with driving and violence, though the evidence is sparse and mostly circumstantial [N3-F3]. More directly, a review of drug-impaired driving notes that methamphetamine users are five times more likely to be killed and over six times more likely to be injured in a traffic crash, with more than double the risk of being killed in a crash when intoxication is present [N3-R2]. These findings are consistent with broader evidence that illicit drugs can increase crash risk and serious injury risk, though methamphetamine’s contribution is not uniquely isolated from other factors [N3-R3].

The evidence also suggests differences by driving setting and exposure timing. The review notes that methamphetamine is especially prevalent in drivers injured in road accidents and in road fatalities, indicating that crash-related exposure timing is often post-accident rather than pre-accident [N3-F3]. Another source emphasizes that methamphetamine can be smoked, snorted, injected, or swallowed, with effects lasting up to 12 hours and onset varying by route: 20–40 minutes after swallowing, 3–5 minutes after snorting, and almost immediately after smoking or injection [N3-F3]. This route and timing heterogeneity implies that crash risk may depend on when methamphetamine is used relative to driving, with acute intoxication likely contributing most during active driving periods.

Contributing risk factors include prior intoxication, co-occurring impairment, and behavioral or cognitive effects. The review explicitly notes that methamphetamine is associated with violence and that the literature is limited by circumstantial and anecdotal evidence [N3-F3]. The driving-under-the-influence review also highlights that studies of driving impairment should assess effects at the highest relevant exposures expected in clinical use, because low to moderate concentrations may not always reflect the worst-case impairment scenario [N2-R2]. This supports the idea that prior intoxication or co-occurring impairment—such as from alcohol, cannabis, or other drugs—can compound methamphetamine effects and increase crash risk. In addition, the evidence base suggests that crash risk is not only due to the drug itself but also to the altered decision-making, attention, and vigilance that methamphetamine may produce [N2-R2].

Overall, the evidence points to an increased risk of crashes and serious injury associated with methamphetamine use, especially when intoxication is present or when exposure occurs shortly before driving [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F3]. However, the literature is limited by small case series, limited epidemiological data, and potential confounding by co-occurring impairment, so the association should be interpreted cautiously [N3-F3][N3-R3].

Direct effects on driving-related cognitive and motor performance are best described as variable and dose-dependent. The evidence indicates that methamphetamine can produce both stimulant/alerting effects at low doses and more disorienting effects at higher doses [N6-R4]. This aligns with the broader driving-under-the-influence review, which states that cognitive tests evaluate attention, perception, memory, and other capacities relevant to safe driving [N2-R5]. At the same time, the evidence also notes that driving impairment studies often do not demonstrate a clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment for many substances, and that statistically significant differences should not be treated as clinically significant per se [N2-F2]. This is important because it cautions against overinterpreting isolated findings.

Impairments in attention, working memory, and reaction time are specifically supported. The driving-under-the-influence review emphasizes that studies should assess effects on attention, divided attention, perception, memory, and other cognitive domains needed for driving [N2-R5]. It also notes that chronic dosing can impair divided attention, coordination, and balance, slow reflexes, and increase reaction time [N2-R4]. This implies that methamphetamine may affect the attentional resources required for monitoring the road, responding to changing stimuli, and maintaining sustained vigilance during driving.

Effects on motor coordination, lane control, and braking response are similarly indicated. The review notes that impaired coordination and balance, slowed reflexes, and increased reaction time are performance effects associated with central nervous system stimulants [N2-R4]. The direct methamphetamine driving study also reports that 0.42 mg/kg d-methamphetamine did not significantly impair simulated driving performance at 2.5 hours post-dose, but the same source emphasizes that these findings must be contextualized within the study’s design and that simulated driving may not fully capture real-world driving behavior [N4-F4]. That caution is relevant because it shows why some studies may find no effect while others report impairment: the timing of assessment, the specific driving tasks, and the pharmacokinetic profile all matter.

Impairment magnitude depends on concentration and individual factors. The evidence highlights that blood concentrations vary widely and that pharmacokinetics are highly individualized, with a mean elimination half-life of about 10 hours and considerable inter-individual variability [N1-F1]. This means that the same dose can produce different concentrations and effects across people. The driving-under-the-influence review also notes that proposed cut-off values vary widely and that detection limits are not universally standardized [N2-F2]. In other words, concentration alone may not be sufficient to infer impairment, because a person’s response depends on dose, route, timing, metabolism, and individual sensitivity [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The same source also notes that chronic use is associated with cognitive impairments and self-regulatory difficulties, which may further degrade driving performance [N2-R2].

In summary, methamphetamine can impair driving-related cognitive and motor performance, especially attention, reaction time, coordination, and balance, but the magnitude of impairment varies by dose, timing, route, and individual factors [N2-R4][N2-R5][N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that some studies may report no effect because the assessment timing, dose level, or driving task does not fully capture the drug’s effects [N4-F4][N2-F2].

Blood concentration data should be interpreted clinically and legally with caution, because the evidence shows that concentration alone is not sufficient to infer impairment. The driving-under-the-influence review explicitly states that there is no unequivocal evidence demonstrating a clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment for many substances and that statistically significant differences should not be considered clinically significant per se [N2-F2]. It also notes that the association between drug concentrations and RTC risk is still debated and that proposed cut-off values vary widely [N2-F2]. This means that a single blood concentration cannot reliably predict impairment in a given driver.

A key limitation is that methamphetamine pharmacokinetics are highly variable. The provided pharmacokinetic evidence shows that the elimination half-life is approximately 10 hours but varies considerably between individuals [N1-F1][N1-R2]. It also shows that elimination half-life is pH-dependent and that methamphetamine concentrations can persist for hours after administration [N1-R3]. This variability means that blood levels may be elevated for some people even after the acute effects have diminished, and conversely, some people may show detectable concentrations despite only minimal pharmacological effects [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Therefore, concentration alone can misclassify impairment: a person may test positive but not be impaired, or may appear impaired at a certain moment without a representative concentration level.

Another limitation is that driving impairment is multifactorial and context-dependent. The driving-under-the-influence review emphasizes that studies should assess effects at the highest relevant exposures expected in clinical use, because low to moderate concentrations may not reflect the worst-case impairment scenario [N2-R2]. It also notes that impaired driving studies often do not demonstrate a clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment and that detection limits are not universally standardized [N2-F2]. This suggests that concentration thresholds are not reliable enforcement tools in themselves, because impairment can occur outside the measured window and because different people may respond differently to the same dose [N2-R2][N2-F2].

Practical recommendations for assessment, prevention, and policy should therefore be evidence-based and context-sensitive. First, assessment should include more than just blood concentration: it should consider route, timing, dose, and individual factors that affect pharmacokinetics [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. Second, prevention efforts should target behaviors that reduce methamphetamine use before driving, such as education, screening, and interventions for drug use disorders [N5-R1][N5-R4]. Third, policy should recognize the limitations of fixed legal thresholds and support more nuanced approaches, such as detection limits or case-specific evaluation, rather than rigid per se prohibitions [N2-F2][N5-R2][N5-R3]. Finally, the evidence suggests that enforcement and clinical decisions should remain cautious in cases where concentration is present but impairment is not clearly established [N2-F2][N5-R2].

In conclusion, blood concentration data should be interpreted as one piece of evidence among many, not as a standalone proof of impairment [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The limitations include inter-individual variability, variable half-life, route-dependent absorption, and the fact that impairment is not strictly dose-dependent in the literature [N1-F1][N1-R2][N2-F2]. The practical implication is that assessment and policy should be flexible, context-aware, and supported by more comprehensive evidence [N2-R2][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Acute versus chronic effects and dose-response patterns show that methamphetamine’s impact on driving and behavior is not uniform. The evidence indicates that low-to-moderate doses can produce stimulant/alerting effects, including arousal, positive mood, cardiac stimulation, and acute improvement in attention and psychomotor coordination [N1-F1]. In contrast, higher doses used typically by illicit users can produce psychosis and acute cardiovascular complications [N1-F1]. This dose-response pattern suggests that low exposure may not necessarily impair driving, while high exposure can worsen cognitive and motor function and increase crash risk [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5].

Acute effects are often described as stimulant-like, with improved psychomotor skills reported at low doses and impaired cognitive performance at higher doses [N2-R1]. The driving-under-the-influence review also notes that chronic dosing can impair divided attention, coordination, and balance, slow reflexes, and increase reaction time [N2-R4]. This means that acute exposure may improve some driving-related skills temporarily, while chronic exposure may degrade them more persistently [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The same source further states that chronic MA use is associated with cognitive impairments, self-regulatory difficulties, and increased aggression [N2-R2]. These findings support the idea that chronic use can compound the risk of impaired driving through both acute and long-term changes in cognition and behavior.

Dose-response relationships across low, moderate, and high exposure are therefore uneven. Low doses may improve some performance domains while still carrying some risk; moderate doses may produce mixed or neutral effects depending on the study design; and high doses are more likely to produce impairment, psychosis, and cardiovascular effects [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4]. The evidence also suggests that some studies report improvement, no effect, or impairment because the study design, dose level, and assessment timing do not fully align with the drug’s pharmacokinetic and behavioral profile [N4-F4][N2-F2]. For example, a methamphetamine driving study found no significant impairment at 2.5 hours post-dose, but that result should be interpreted in context rather than as proof of absence of effect [N4-F4].

Why some studies report improvement, no effect, or impairment is explained by several factors. First, the pharmacokinetic profile means that concentration varies by route, dose, and timing, so the same dose can produce different effects in different people and at different times [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. Second, the literature is heterogeneous, with some studies finding no clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment and others reporting impairment [N2-F2]. Third, simulated driving may not fully capture real-world driving behavior, which is why some studies may find no effect while others report impairment [N4-F4][N2-R5]. Finally, individual factors such as prior intoxication, co-occurring impairment, and cognitive reserve can alter how a person responds to methamphetamine [N2-R2][N3-R2]. 

Overall, the evidence points to an acute dose-response pattern where low doses can sometimes improve performance and higher doses can impair performance, while chronic use adds persistent cognitive and behavioral deficits that may further degrade driving outcomes [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4]. The dose-response relationship is therefore not linear, and the interpretation of individual studies should take into account study design, dose level, timing, and individual variability [N4-F4][N2-F2].

## How do varying blood concentrations of methamphetamine affect driving performance and the associated risks?

Methamphetamine’s effects on driving performance and crash risk depend on blood concentration, dose, route, timing, and individual differences, but the relationship is not simple or linear. The evidence shows that low-to-moderate concentrations may sometimes produce stimulant-like effects, while higher concentrations are more likely to impair driving and increase crash risk. Importantly, blood concentration alone is not a reliable standalone indicator of impairment, because pharmacokinetics vary widely and impairment is context-dependent [N1-F1][N2-F2][N1-R2][N1-R3].

### 1) Biological and dose-related context for methamphetamine concentrations

The pharmacokinetic profile of methamphetamine is central to interpreting concentration-based assessments. The mean elimination half-life is approximately 10 hours, but there is considerable inter-individual variability, and elimination half-life is also pH-dependent, with methamphetamine ranging from 6 to 15 hours and amphetamine from 7 to 34 hours [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means that blood concentrations do not remain constant after ingestion and can vary substantially between people.

Typical concentration ranges are not uniformly reported in the provided evidence, but the available material suggests that concentrations can vary widely. One study reports mean blood and saliva d,l-methamphetamine concentrations of approximately 90 ng/ml at 2 hours and 95 ng/ml at 3 hours after 0.42 mg/kg oral administration [N4-F4]. Another source notes that methamphetamine can be smoked, snorted, injected, or swallowed, with effects lasting up to 12 hours and onset varying by route: 20–40 minutes after swallowing, 3–5 minutes after snorting, and almost immediately after smoking or injection [N3-F3]. This route and timing heterogeneity means that blood concentrations can differ widely depending on how the drug is taken.

The evidence also highlights that thresholds for measurable pharmacological effects versus intoxication are not neatly separable. Low-to-moderate doses may produce arousal, positive mood, cardiac stimulation, and acute improvement in cognitive domains such as attention and psychomotor coordination, whereas higher doses can produce psychosis and acute cardiovascular complications [N1-F1]. This indicates that the same person can experience different effects at different concentrations, and that concentration alone does not determine whether driving impairment is present [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

### 2) Direct effects on driving-related cognitive and motor performance

## How do varying blood concentrations of methamphetamine affect driving performance and the associated risks?

Methamphetamine’s effects on driving performance and crash risk depend on blood concentration, dose, route, timing, and individual differences, but the relationship is not simple or linear. The evidence shows that low-to-moderate concentrations may sometimes produce stimulant-like effects, while higher concentrations are more likely to impair driving and increase crash risk. Importantly, blood concentration alone is not a reliable standalone indicator of impairment, because pharmacokinetics vary widely and impairment is context-dependent [N1-F1][N2-F2][N1-R2][N1-R3].

### 1) Biological and dose-related context for methamphetamine concentrations

The pharmacokinetic profile of methamphetamine is central to interpreting concentration-based assessments. The mean elimination half-life is approximately 10 hours, but there is considerable inter-individual variability, and elimination half-life is also pH-dependent, with methamphetamine ranging from 6 to 15 hours and amphetamine from 7 to 34 hours [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means that blood concentrations do not remain constant after ingestion and can vary substantially between people.

Typical concentration ranges are not uniformly reported in the provided evidence, but the available material suggests that concentrations can vary widely. One study reports mean blood and saliva d,l-methamphetamine concentrations of approximately 90 ng/ml at 2 hours and 95 ng/ml at 3 hours after 0.42 mg/kg oral administration [N4-F4]. Another source notes that methamphetamine can be smoked, snorted, injected, or swallowed, with effects lasting up to 12 hours and onset varying by route: 20–40 minutes after swallowing, 3–5 minutes after snorting, and almost immediately after smoking or injection [N3-F3]. This route and timing heterogeneity means that blood concentrations can differ widely depending on how the drug is taken.

The evidence also highlights that thresholds for measurable pharmacological effects versus intoxication are not neatly separable. Low-to-moderate doses may produce arousal, positive mood, cardiac stimulation, and acute improvement in cognitive domains such as attention and psychomotor coordination, whereas higher doses can produce psychosis and acute cardiovascular complications [N1-F1]. This indicates that the same person can experience different effects at different concentrations, and that concentration alone does not determine whether driving impairment is present [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

### 2) Direct effects on driving-related cognitive and motor performance

Methamphetamine can impair driving-related cognitive and motor performance, but the magnitude of impairment varies by dose, timing, route, and individual factors. The evidence indicates that methamphetamine can produce both stimulant/alerting effects at low doses and more disorienting effects at higher doses [N6-R4]. This aligns with the broader driving-under-the-influence review, which states that cognitive tests evaluate attention, perception, memory, and other capacities relevant to safe driving [N2-R5].

Impairments in attention, working memory, and reaction time are specifically supported. The driving-under-the-influence review emphasizes that studies should assess effects on attention, divided attention, perception, memory, and other cognitive domains needed for driving [N2-R5]. It also notes that chronic dosing can impair divided attention, coordination, and balance, slow reflexes, and increase reaction time [N2-R4]. This implies that methamphetamine may affect the attentional resources required for monitoring the road, responding to changing stimuli, and maintaining sustained vigilance during driving.

Effects on motor coordination, lane control, and braking response are similarly indicated. The review notes that impaired coordination and balance, slowed reflexes, and increased reaction time are performance effects associated with central nervous system stimulants [N2-R4]. The direct methamphetamine driving study also reports that 0.42 mg/kg d-methamphetamine did not significantly impair simulated driving performance at 2.5 hours post-dose, but the same source emphasizes that these findings must be contextualized within the study’s design and that simulated driving may not fully capture real-world driving behavior [N4-F4]. That caution is relevant because it shows why some studies may find no effect while others report impairment: the timing of assessment, the specific driving tasks, and the pharmacokinetic profile all matter.

Impairment magnitude depends on concentration and individual factors. The evidence highlights that blood concentrations vary widely and that pharmacokinetics are highly individualized, with a mean elimination half-life of about 10 hours and considerable inter-individual variability [N1-F1]. This means that the same dose can produce different concentrations and effects across people. The driving-under-the-influence review also notes that proposed cut-off values vary widely and that detection limits are not universally standardized [N2-F2]. In other words, concentration alone may not be sufficient to infer impairment, because a person’s response depends on dose, route, timing, metabolism, and individual sensitivity [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The same source also notes that chronic use is associated with cognitive impairments and self-regulatory difficulties, which may further degrade driving performance [N2-R2].

### 3) Risk of crashes and real-world safety consequences

Evidence linking methamphetamine use to crash or incident rates is mixed but suggestive of increased risk overall. A 1996 study of 28 cases of drivers arrested or killed in traffic accidents who tested positive for methamphetamine concluded that methamphetamine was implicated in those outcomes [N3-R1]. Another review of injury literature reports that methamphetamine is associated with driving and violence, though the evidence is sparse and mostly circumstantial [N3-F3]. More directly, a review of drug-impaired driving notes that methamphetamine users are five times more likely to be killed and over six times more likely to be injured in a traffic crash, with more than double the risk of being killed in a crash when intoxication is present [N3-R2]. These findings are consistent with broader evidence that illicit drugs can increase crash risk and serious injury risk, though methamphetamine’s contribution is not uniquely isolated from other factors [N3-R3].

The evidence also suggests differences by driving setting and exposure timing. The review notes that methamphetamine is especially prevalent in drivers injured in road accidents and in road fatalities, indicating that crash-related exposure timing is often post-accident rather than pre-accident [N3-F3]. Another source emphasizes that methamphetamine can be smoked, snorted, injected, or swallowed, with effects lasting up to 12 hours and onset varying by route: 20–40 minutes after swallowing, 3–5 minutes after snorting, and almost immediately after smoking or injection [N3-F3]. This route and timing heterogeneity implies that crash risk may depend on when methamphetamine is used relative to driving, with acute intoxication likely contributing most during active driving periods.

Contributing risk factors include prior intoxication, co-occurring impairment, and behavioral or cognitive effects. The review explicitly notes that methamphetamine is associated with violence and that the literature is limited by circumstantial and anecdotal evidence [N3-F3]. The driving-under-the-influence review also highlights that studies of driving impairment should assess effects at the highest relevant exposures expected in clinical use, because low to moderate concentrations may not always reflect the worst-case impairment scenario [N2-R2]. This supports the idea that prior intoxication or co-occurring impairment—such as from alcohol, cannabis, or other drugs—can compound methamphetamine effects and increase crash risk. In addition, the evidence base suggests that crash risk is not only due to the drug itself but also to the altered decision-making, attention, and vigilance that methamphetamine may produce [N2-R2].

### 4) Interpretation and practical implications

Blood concentration data should be interpreted clinically and legally with caution, because the evidence shows that concentration alone is not sufficient to infer impairment. The driving-under-the-influence review explicitly states that there is no unequivocal evidence demonstrating a clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment for many substances and that statistically significant differences should not be considered clinically significant per se [N2-F2]. It also notes that the association between drug concentrations and RTC risk is still debated and that proposed cut-off values vary widely [N2-F2]. This means that a single blood concentration cannot reliably predict impairment in a given driver.

A key limitation is that methamphetamine pharmacokinetics are highly variable. The provided pharmacokinetic evidence shows that the elimination half-life is approximately 10 hours but varies considerably between individuals [N1-F1][N1-R2]. It also shows that elimination half-life is pH-dependent and that methamphetamine concentrations can persist for hours after administration [N1-R3]. This variability means that blood levels may be elevated for some people even after the acute effects have diminished, and conversely, some people may show detectable concentrations despite only minimal pharmacological effects [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Therefore, concentration alone can misclassify impairment: a person may test positive but not be impaired, or may appear impaired at a certain moment without a representative concentration level [N1-F1][N1-R3].

Another limitation is that driving impairment is multifactorial and context-dependent. The driving-under-the-influence review emphasizes that studies should assess effects at the highest relevant exposures expected in clinical use, because low to moderate concentrations may not reflect the worst-case impairment scenario [N2-R2]. It also notes that impaired driving studies often do not demonstrate a clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment and that detection limits are not universally standardized [N2-F2]. This suggests that concentration thresholds are not reliable enforcement tools in themselves, because impairment can occur outside the measured window and because different people may respond differently to the same dose [N2-R2][N2-F2].

Practical recommendations for assessment, prevention, and policy should therefore be evidence-based and context-sensitive. First, assessment should include more than just blood concentration: it should consider route, timing, dose, and individual factors that affect pharmacokinetics [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. Second, prevention efforts should target behaviors that reduce methamphetamine use before driving, such as education, screening, and interventions for drug use disorders [N5-R1][N5-R4]. Third, policy should recognize the limitations of fixed legal thresholds and support more nuanced approaches, such as detection limits or case-specific evaluation, rather than rigid per se prohibitions [N2-F2][N5-R2][N5-R3]. Finally, the evidence suggests that enforcement and clinical decisions should remain cautious in cases where concentration is present but impairment is not clearly established [N2-F2][N5-R2].

### 5) Acute versus chronic effects and dose-response patterns

Acute versus chronic effects and dose-response patterns show that methamphetamine’s impact on driving and behavior is not uniform. The evidence indicates that low-to-moderate doses can produce stimulant/alerting effects, including arousal, positive mood, cardiac stimulation, and acute improvement in attention and psychomotor coordination [N1-F1]. In contrast, higher doses used typically by illicit users can produce psychosis and acute cardiovascular complications [N1-F1]. This dose-response pattern suggests that low exposure may not necessarily impair driving, while high exposure can worsen cognitive and motor function and increase crash risk [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5].

Acute effects are often described as stimulant-like, with improved psychomotor skills reported at low doses and impaired cognitive performance at higher doses [N2-R1]. The driving-under-the-influence review also notes that chronic dosing can impair divided attention, coordination, and balance, slow reflexes, and increase reaction time [N2-R4]. This means that acute exposure may improve some driving-related skills temporarily, while chronic exposure may degrade them more persistently [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The same source further states that chronic MA use is associated with cognitive impairments, self-regulatory difficulties, and increased aggression [N2-R2]. These findings support the idea that chronic use can compound the risk of impaired driving through both acute and long-term changes in cognition and behavior.

Dose-response relationships across low, moderate, and high exposure are therefore uneven. Low doses may improve some performance domains while still carrying some risk; moderate doses may produce mixed or neutral effects depending on the study design; and high doses are more likely to produce impairment, psychosis, and cardiovascular effects [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4]. The evidence also suggests that some studies report improvement, no effect, or impairment because the study design, dose level, and assessment timing do not fully align with the drug’s pharmacokinetic and behavioral profile [N4-F4][N2-F2]. For example, a methamphetamine driving study found no significant impairment at 2.5 hours post-dose, but that result should be interpreted in context rather than as proof of absence of effect [N4-F4].

Why some studies report improvement, no effect, or impairment is explained by several factors. First, the pharmacokinetic profile means that concentration varies by route, dose, and timing, so the same dose can produce different effects in different people and at different times [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. Second, the literature is heterogeneous, with some studies finding no clear dose/concentration-dependent impairment and others reporting impairment [N2-F2]. Third, simulated driving may not fully capture real-world driving behavior, which is why some studies may find no effect while others report impairment [N4-F4][N2-R5]. Finally, individual factors such as prior intoxication, co-occurring impairment, and cognitive reserve can alter how a person responds to methamphetamine [N2-R2][N3-R2].

### 6) Integrated conclusion

In short, varying blood concentrations of methamphetamine affect driving performance and associated risks in a dose-dependent, context-dependent, and individual-dependent way. Lower concentrations may sometimes produce stimulant-like effects, while higher concentrations are more likely to impair attention, reaction time, coordination, and braking response and increase crash risk [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The evidence also shows that crash risk is increased when intoxication is present or when exposure occurs shortly before driving, and that prior intoxication or co-occurring impairment can compound the risk [N3-R1][N3-R2][N2-R2].

However, blood concentration alone is not sufficient to infer impairment. Methamphetamine pharmacokinetics are highly variable, and proposed cut-off values differ widely, so concentration should be interpreted cautiously in clinical and legal settings [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F2]. Practical recommendations include using context-sensitive assessment, targeting prevention before driving, and supporting more nuanced policy approaches rather than rigid thresholds [N2-F2][N5-R2][N5-R3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that methamphetamine concentrations are an important but incomplete signal for impairment and crash risk, and that driving decisions should be based on a broader evaluation of dose, timing, route, individual factors, and real-world behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2].
